Jean-Paul Marat. Born in 1743, this radical journalist and physician was a driving force behind the French Revolution's most violent phase. He founded and edited L'Ami du Peuple, The Friend of the People, a radical newspaper that called for mass executions of suspected enemies and royalist sympathizers. As a deputy to the National Convention, he was a powerful voice on the Mountain, the radical faction, demanding purges and violence. Marat suffered from a chronic skin disease, likely dermatitis, that confined him to a medicinal bath. He worked from that bath even during political meetings, reinforcing his image as a martyr devoted entirely to the cause. He accused the Girondins, the moderate republicans, of betraying the revolution and pushed hard for their arrest and execution in June 1793. On July 13, 1793, he was assassinated in his bath by Charlotte Corday, a royalist sympathizer. His death made him a revolutionary icon. His funeral was a massive public ceremony, and his image was immortalized in paintings and revolutionary propaganda as the Friend of the People. His radicalism and his cult of personality accelerated the revolution's turn toward systematic terror. He died in 1793, but his influence lasted long after.
